topic.title: The farewell email
topic.claim: The nicest things your company will ever say about you are in replies to your farewell email.
topic.moment: 'Will miss you so much, you were the backbone of this team' from someone who never replied to your messages.

turn.actually: Praise is free once you're leaving, because it can no longer cost anyone a rating or a raise.

topic.because: While you stay, praise has to be paid for in money and promotions. On your last day it costs nothing.
topic.payoff: If they only called you the backbone on your way out, they knew it all along.
topic.behaviour: Colleagues reply-all with warm tributes to someone whose appraisal they rated average.
topic.mechanism: Praise has a price only while it can turn into a raise.
topic.group: Anyone who has switched jobs at least once
topic.send_to: The friend serving notice period right now.
topic.why_now: Job-switch season is constant, and everyone has read or written one of these recently.

score.why: Farewell praise is free because it can no longer cost a rating or a raise. It's dry, human and shareable.

topic.villain: a rating system where praise is free only once you can no longer be rated

ledger.text: Praise from a manager or colleague carries an implicit cost while someone is still employed, because it could translate into a better performance rating, a promotion, or a raise that has to be approved; once that person is leaving, the same praise requires no such approval or payout, so it costs nothing to give.
ledger.sentence: While you stayed, calling you the backbone had a price. It could turn into a better rating, a promotion, a raise someone had to sign. On your way out, the same sentence costs nothing. Nobody has to pay for it anymore.

mechanism.actual_mechanism: Performance ratings feed a merit matrix drawn against a fixed merit-increase budget pool (commonly ~3-4% of payroll), so rating one person higher genuinely consumes a limited shared pool and must clear calibration sign-off and budget approval before any raise or promotion is granted. A farewell reply-all compliment touches none of these instruments: once someone has resigned they can no longer be rated, placed in the merit matrix, or promoted, so the praise has no budget line it could trigger. The factual premises — that in-cycle acknowledgment can translate into an approval-gated, budget-constrained payout while exit praise cannot — both hold.

sources.quote: The pool stays fixed once the company sets it. If managers recommend increases equal to 5% of payroll against a 3% budget, compensation has to bring the recommendations back to 3%.

Without calibration, a lenient manager might give all ten of their direct reports 'exceeds expectations' ratings, consuming a disproportionate share of the merit pool... Budget distribution cannot go out until the calibration session for each function is signed off by the relevant HRBP.
Merit-based pay uses a structured process to determine how much of a raise each employee receives based on their performance rating... calibrated to their performance rating and budget.

cover.headline: The nicest thing they'll ever call you lands in your [farewell replies]
cover.sub: From the person who left you on seen for two years.

paragraphs: The nicest thing they'll ever call you lands in your farewell replies.
slides.why_swipe: The reader wants to see their own last-day inbox.

paragraphs: It's your second-last day. You line up the farewell email, the one about the chai breaks and the memories, and hit send at 6pm.
The laptop is warm on your knees. You close the lid, half expecting silence.
slides.why_swipe: What came back after they hit send?

paragraphs: Then the replies start. Reply-all, one after another, the little pings stacking up.
"Will miss you so much, you were the backbone of this team."
It's from the person who left your messages on seen for two years.
slides.why_swipe: Is that praise finally honest, or is something off?

paragraphs: So scroll up in the same inbox. Six months ago, that same person filled out your appraisal.
"Meets expectations." Average. Nothing that moved your number.
**The backbone of the team got a middle rating.**
slides.why_swipe: Why was the praise cheap then and flowing now?

paragraphs: Here's the part. While you stayed, calling you the backbone had a price. It could turn into a better rating, a promotion, a raise someone had to sign.
On your way out, the same sentence costs nothing. Nobody has to pay for it anymore.
slides.why_swipe: So what does that make the whole warm thread?

paragraphs: They didn't suddenly see your worth on the last day. They saw it the whole time.
**It just finally became free to say so.**

A farewell reply-all compliment touches none of these instruments: once someone has resigned they can no longer be rated, placed in the merit matrix, or promoted, so the praise has no budget line it could trigger. The factual premises — that in-cycle acknowledgment can translate into an approval-gated, budget-constrained payout while exit praise cannot — both hold.

Merit-based pay uses a structured process to determine how much of a raise each employee receives based on their performance rating... calibrated to their performance rating and budget.
